scout.purpose: Functions turn a growing program into named, reusable decisions with clear inputs and outputs.
scout.realWorldUse: Android projects use functions for validation, state updates, formatting, mapping data, event handling, and nearly every interaction with a library.
scout.outcome: Declare, call, and decompose functions using parameters, return types, defaults, and named arguments.

blocks.text: A function has a name, zero or more parameters, a return type, and a body. Parameters describe the inputs available to the body. A return value communicates the result to the caller. Read fun calculateTotal(quantity: Int, price: Double): Double as a contract: provide an Int and a Double, and receive a Double. Kotlin function parameters are read-only inside the body, which prevents the function from quietly replacing the caller’s input names.

sections.title: Return a value or perform an action

blocks.text: A short function that returns one expression can use an expression body: fun isValid(amount: Double) = amount > 0.0. The compiler infers the return type, although explicit return types are valuable for public APIs because they preserve the intended contract. A function that only performs an action returns Unit. Unit means the call completes without producing a meaningful domain result; it is not the same as failure or absence.

blocks.caption: One function answers a question; the other performs output and implicitly returns Unit.

blocks.title: Return facts before printing them
blocks.text: Business rules are easier to reuse and test when they return values. Keep console or UI presentation at an outer boundary.

sections.title: Make calls clear and responsibilities small

blocks.text: A default parameter supplies a value when the caller omits that argument. Named arguments make calls self-documenting and allow selected defaults to be skipped. They are especially useful for adjacent arguments of the same type or unexplained Boolean flags. Defaults should represent a safe, unsurprising common case. A function with too many configuration parameters may be revealing that several responsibilities or concepts need their own model.

blocks.caption: Defaults keep the common call short while names make each supplied argument unambiguous.

blocks.text: A useful function does one coherent job at one level of abstraction. “Validate an amount” and “format an approved expense” are separate responsibilities even if one screen needs both. Decomposition is not about making every line a function. It is about giving important rules names, reducing duplication, and allowing the caller to understand the program as a sequence of meaningful operations.

trap_check.mistake: Printing a calculated result inside every business function.
trap_check.why: The result becomes difficult to reuse in a UI, test, or another calculation.
trap_check.fix: Return the value and let an outer boundary decide how to present it.

trap_check.mistake: Using multiple unexplained Boolean positional arguments.
trap_check.why: A call such as format(value, true, false) hides what each Boolean controls.
trap_check.fix: Use named arguments or replace flags with a clearer model.

challenge_intro.task: Refactor one expense script into separate validation, calculation, and formatting functions.
challenge_intro.successLooksLike: Each function has a clear contract, business functions return values, and main reads as a short coordination flow.

recall.prompt: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
recall.answer: A parameter is declared by the function; an argument is supplied by a caller.
The function completes an action without returning a meaningful domain value.
They expose which parameter each value supplies and clarify otherwise ambiguous calls.
